subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows
passage:
Looking back at my first four months as lead, I can see it happening, though I didn't then.
In meetings I started saying, 'As I decided in March…' or 'Remember when I pushed for the new vendor?' Not once. Often. I liked it when the room went quiet while I talked. I liked that people waited for me to finish.
When Vaibhav's plan for the dashboard went well, I told the director it was 'the approach I'd set'. It sort of was. Mostly it was Vaibhav's.
The odd part was how praise changed. In the first weeks, a 'well done' from my manager made my day. By June I noticed I was annoyed when one didn't come. When Vaibhav presented and didn't mention me, I was irritated for the whole afternoon.
I thought it meant I was confident now. I'm not sure it did.
— Yamini

qa.q: What did Yamini tell the director about Vaibhav's dashboard plan?
qa.a: Yamini told the director it was 'the approach I'd set'.

qa.q: What did Yamini feel when Vaibhav presented and didn't mention the lead?
qa.a: Yamini felt irritated for the whole afternoon, showing that praise had turned into an expectation.

qa.q: What could Yamini do differently when a teammate's work goes well?
qa.a: Yamini could credit Vaibhav clearly by name to the director, and ask whether team members feel heard in meetings.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav feel hearing the plan described as 'the approach I'd set'?
qa.a: Vaibhav might feel overlooked and less motivated, since that work was quietly claimed.

grounding: It shows a new lead beginning to see themself as the smart one, quoting past decisions, enjoying deference and coming to expect praise.

subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows
passage:
Note for file: leadership check-in. Written by Charu, department head.
Rekha (26) took over the analytics team in January. The team's output is steady. But I've noticed a pattern over the last six weeks.
In Monday reviews Rekha refers to her own earlier calls several times per meeting: 'This is why I chose the cloud setup,' 'Like I said last year.' When juniors suggest something, she often waits a beat, then restates it as her idea.
In the corridor she looks pleased when people stop talking as she passes. Last week, when I thanked the team for the quarterly report without naming her first, she came to my cabin afterwards and asked, lightly but not quite lightly, whether I'd 'forgotten who ran it'.
She is good at this job. I don't want to lose that.
Next step: a one-to-one on Thursday. I'll ask her how she thinks the team sees her meetings, and listen before I say anything.

qa.q: Which team did Rekha take over in January?
qa.a: Rekha took over the analytics team in January.

qa.q: What does Rekha's question about whether Charu had 'forgotten who ran it' suggest about Rekha's mood?
qa.a: It suggests she was hurt and irritated not to be named first, and has started to expect praise.

qa.q: What turning point could Charu's Thursday one-to-one offer Rekha?
qa.a: Asking how the team sees her meetings could help Rekha notice the pattern herself before it hardens, and start crediting others.

qa.q: How might the juniors in Rekha's team be affected when she restates their ideas as hers?
qa.a: They may feel unseen and stop sharing ideas, since their suggestions end up as the lead's.

grounding: It shows a new lead who increasingly sees herself as the smart one, quotes her past decisions, enjoys deference and comes to expect praise.

subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows
passage:
Three months after becoming lead, Farhan had developed a habit. Whenever the team debated anything in the Hyderabad office, he'd lean back and say, "Remember when I pushed for the cache layer last year? Everyone said no. I was right."
It had been a good call. It had also come up in six meetings this month.
He liked how the room went quiet when he started speaking now. He liked that Neelam, who used to argue with him over lunch, now said, "Whatever you think, Farhan." He didn't notice she said it with less energy each time.
On Friday Neelam presented a fix that cut load times by half. The director praised her in front of everyone. Farhan clapped, then sat through the rest of the meeting with a tight jaw. Nobody had mentioned that he approved the approach. He found himself waiting, all evening, for someone to say it.

qa.q: What decision does Farhan keep bringing up?
qa.a: When he pushed for the cache layer last year.

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling when the director praised Neelam?
qa.a: He felt irritated and overlooked, expecting credit for approving the approach, which shows praise turning into an expectation.

qa.q: What could Farhan notice to catch this change in himself?
qa.a: That he mentioned the cache layer six times this month and waited all evening for credit; asking Neelam for her honest view would help.

qa.q: How does Neelam experience Farhan as a lead?
qa.a: Neelam has gone from arguing freely to saying 'whatever you think' with less energy, suggesting she feels less heard.

grounding: A new lead begins to see himself as the smart one, quotes his old decision, enjoys deference and starts to expect praise.

subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows
passage:
"Guess what the intern said today?" Imran asked, spooning biryani. "He said, 'Sir, how did you know the bug was in the queue?'"
"Sir?" Afreen raised an eyebrow. "Since when do they call you sir?"
"Since I became lead. I didn't ask them to. They just do." He smiled. "Honestly, I'm usually the smartest one in those rooms now."
"Usually?"
"Mostly. Remember the migration I planned last year? Still the best decision anyone's made on that team."
"You've told me about the migration four times this week."
"Because it's relevant!"
"And yesterday, when your director didn't comment on your slides, you sulked all evening."
"I did not sulk. I just expected... something. Some acknowledgement."
"You used to be happy when anyone said thank you. Now you're upset when they don't."
Imran put down his spoon. "That's not fair."
"Maybe. Think about it anyway."

qa.q: What did the intern call Imran?
qa.a: Sir.

qa.q: What does Imran's sulking over the director's silence show about how he feels?
qa.a: He feels hurt and entitled, since praise has shifted from a welcome surprise to something he expects.

qa.q: What could Imran do with Afreen's observation?
qa.a: Instead of defending himself, he could notice how often he quotes the migration and how he reacts when no one praises him.

qa.q: How does Afreen see the change in Imran?
qa.a: Afreen sees him becoming vain and harder to please, and cares enough to say so honestly, even at the risk of a quarrel.

grounding: A new lead at home boasts of being the smartest, quotes his old decision, enjoys being called sir and now expects praise.

subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows
passage:
I can see it now, looking back at my first six months as creative lead, though at the time I'd have called it confidence. I began opening every review with "When I did the tea campaign..." as if everyone hadn't heard it. When juniors went quiet as I spoke, I read it as respect, and I liked it more than I'd admit.
The turning moment was small. Nirmala, who joined with me and used to tease me mercilessly, pitched an idea better than mine. The client loved it. And my first feeling wasn't pride in my team. It was a sour, childish thought: but I'm the lead.
That evening I understood I'd started expecting praise in every meeting, the way you expect the lights to come on when you press the switch. Missing it felt like an insult.
I'm Deepika. I'm not proud of that phase, but I'm glad I caught myself in it.

qa.q: How did Deepika open every review?
qa.a: With 'When I did the tea campaign...'

qa.q: What was Deepika feeling when the client loved Nirmala's idea?
qa.a: Deepika felt a sour, childish jealousy, thinking 'but I'm the lead', instead of pride in the team.

qa.q: What could Deepika do now that the pattern is clear?
qa.a: Stop quoting the old campaign, credit Nirmala openly, and ask the juniors why they go quiet.

qa.q: How might Nirmala experience Deepika's change?
qa.a: Nirmala may feel distanced and less free to tease or challenge as before, even as Nirmala's ideas win.

grounding: A new creative lead looks back on seeing themself as the smart one, quoting past work, enjoying deference and expecting praise.

subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows
passage:
Manager's note, one-to-one prep, Friday.
Rashmi has been team lead for three months, and delivery is strong. But I've noticed a change. In Tuesday's design review she said "As I decided back in March" three times. When Karan questioned her caching choice, she smiled, said "Let's trust experience here," and moved on. The juniors now wait for her view before speaking, and she seems to enjoy it. When I thanked the team for the release, she looked slightly put out that her name wasn't first. Three months ago she credited the juniors before herself. I don't think she sees it yet. At our one-to-one on Monday I'll praise the results, then ask how she makes room for disagreement, and share Karan's point about caching, which was a good one.
Sudha

qa.q: What phrase did Rashmi repeat three times in the design review?
qa.a: "As I decided back in March."

qa.q: What does Rashmi's reaction to the team thanks suggest about how she now feels?
qa.a: She seems a little hurt and put out, expecting praise to come to her first, as if it were now her due.

qa.q: What turning point does the manager plan for Monday?
qa.a: Praising the results but asking how Rashmi makes room for disagreement, and sharing Karan's good point about caching.

qa.q: What might Karan feel after being brushed off?
qa.a: Karan probably feels dismissed and frustrated, since a good point was waved away with "trust experience".

grounding: Shows a new lead quoting past decisions, enjoying deference and coming to expect praise, as noticed by the manager.
